as a seed in ensuring our full participation in the implementation and enforcement of the treaty. Mr. Chairman, it is unfortunate that we are leaving Busan without a concluded treaty. Thank you, Chair. Distinguished Chair, thank you very much for giving me the floor. This issue is of key importance, and of course, there's a need to combine our efforts in coming up with global recommendations to ensure ecological and rational use of plastics, including the increasing risks with regard to people's health and plastic pollution and the increasing volume of plastic waste. What's important here is that sustainable development and the well-being of individuals goes hand in hand with ecological sustainability. For example, the 12 SDGs with regard to sustainable or SDG 12 rather with regard to sustainable manufacturing. Here we should draw particular attention to the management of waste, use of modern technologies, and thinking of how we use plastics, respecting common but differentiated responsibilities principle. I'd like to note here that in order to ensure the best results in combating plastic pollution, we need to take into account the views of business and the private sector. For example, in the first statement that we made with regard to Monday, the outcome document must be adopted on a consensus basis. This is important because it's the only way that we can ensure equal opportunities for all countries. Kazakhstan is a country with a burgeoning economy and it is a landlocked country. Our impact on the environment, in particular on the sea and maritime pollution, is minimal. However, there is an increased risk, of course, for the burgeoning manufacturing and companies of Kazakhstan. So anything that is linked to the production or a limitation of the production would, of course, limit our economic stability and our development, which is an ideal. So I believe that there are many countries that share my view here. I would note that Kazakhstan, like other countries, is a responsible country which considers the contribution to plastic pollution, especially in the maritime environment. That's why we need to take into account the primary plastics production and the Kazakhstan proposal that we've made with regards to the first paragraph of the goals and principles of the agreement. Our proposal here is very simple. With regards to plastic pollution, that should be looked at with regard to, hand in hand with regard to social and economic development. We want to see in Article 11 as well, with regard to the financing, something particularly reflected here. It's important to have support for developing countries. We have to have equal opportunities to ensure the best results for a global arrival at the limitation of plastic pollution. We need to have flexible mechanisms which are transparent. because otherwise we'll have an uncontrolled process. We need to have a search for a constructive, mutually beneficial outcome which would help all. The international recommendations should stimulate countries to developing their own national programs to regulate the import and export of plastic production, first and foremost aimed at limiting, of course, environmental pollution. That should be the goal, and we should have a transitional period which will allow us to improve our scientific approaches to this issue, and also to search for alternatives to plastics. We're prepared to work on the document which has been proposed, as long as we see the reflection in it of our own proposal and balanced approach, which will take into account pollution, yes, but also human health on the other hand, and socioeconomic development, as I've mentioned. Still, we are exposed to the harms of continuous plastic production and lack of support for reuse solutions. At the start of the plastic treaty negotiations, we thought you had everything you needed to develop a strong, legally binding agreement to tackle the pollution associated with the entire life cycle of plastics. Most member states supported ambitious measures to cut plastic production and eliminate harmful chemicals. Yet, despite this unity, the talks here in Busan have stalled, held back by the few resistant voices. We have witnessed how the interests of a select few have been prioritized over the long-term health and well-being of our future and people. And we are outraged. Now again we ask you, do not let us down. When ambitious countries refuse to accept weak treaty, our movement stands with them. We are committed to end plastic pollution, but please do not shift the full responsibility again to our communities and our generation. Please do not let the interest of spoilers outweigh the long-term interests of our planet and our citizens. We demand a more ambitious and implementable treaty that will truly solve the plastic pollution crisis, cut production, eliminate problematic plastics and toxic chemicals, and waste colonialism, and institute genuine measures also solutions to resolve plastic crisis. I believe you have empathy and love in your hearts. We can create more kindness than evil in humanity for our future. Thank you.

The full life cycle of plastics is not adequately covered, including chemicals, which cannot be addressed in other binding treaties, such as the Stockholm Convention on POPs. We urge that reference to the individual and collective rights of Indigenous Peoples, including the rights to self-determination and full and effective participation, as is affirmed in the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, are included in the treaty text. Thank you, Chair. The Endocrine Society appreciates the progress and ambition through the Chair's series of nonpapers. As the INC continues deliberations, we stress the importance of establishing mandatory lists of chemicals of concern in Article 3. The lists in the current nonpaper are rightly focused on children's unique susceptibility, but all populations are exposed at levels considered unsafe. We note the European Food Safety Agency recent decision following a systematic review of bisphenol A, indicating that the only safe approach is a ban. We strongly support an approach that applies positive hazard data from one chemical to others in the same group. Importantly, the scientists participating in the review committee identified in Article 3 should disclose potential conflicts of interest. and processes should be in place to manage perceived and actual conflicts. Engagement of scientists and other knowledge holders free from conflicts is essential for the treaty to be recognized as unbiased and trusted. We are concerned that continued production of plastic will increase the danger to human and environmental health and urge members to agree upon measures to limit production. Increases in chronic disease globally, and especially in low and middle income countries, will continue unless explicit limits on plastic production are included in Article 6. We urge ongoing refinement of Article 17 and 18 to address the need for biomonitoring studies to evaluate human exposure. The treaty's success is in part dependent on measurable reductions in chemical body burden, which will improve public health. Industrializing countries should be supported through resources, including expertise, to participate in studies. Finally, we urge members to find convergence on the inclusion of human and environmental health, particularly through Article 19, but also throughout the treaty. The costs of inaction are real, reaching $250 billion annually in the US alone. Human exposure to fluoropolymer chemicals has caused 400,000 babies each year to be born with a low birth weight, predominantly from Asian regions. We must therefore follow the instructions given by the robust body of evidence. Whether we call nanoplastics and chemicals used in plastics leakage or waste or exposures by design, plastic pollution is a human health issue. We thank the chair.
